body.text: AI and smart glasses emerge as threats to Asia's famously tough exams
In short:
South Korean authorities have taken extraordinary measures to detect cheating in the country's high-stakes university entrance exam.
A 34-year-old man's confession to cheating on a separate exam threw preparations for the College Scholastic Ability Test, or "Suneung", into panic.
AI and wearable devices have emerged as risks for exams across Asia, where test scores can determine life trajectories.
Three alarms sounded on South Korean smartphones as students sat the nation's gruelling, eight-hour university entrance exam last week.
Authorities used a nationwide mobile phone alert, usually reserved for disaster warnings, to catch students who smuggled devices into the marathon exam.
It was one of several measures to prevent cheating after a 34-year-old South Korean man's confession on YouTube threw preparations for the College Scholastic Ability Test, or "Suneung", into panic.
Days before the Suneung, Han Won-seok, who had achieved unusually high marks in a separate national tax accountancy exam, admitted to cheating.
The student said he used a hidden micro camera and smartphone to get answers from artificial intelligence.

The confession raised fears that the country was ill-prepared to detect similar cheating in the high-stakes Suneung, and the government went to extraordinary lengths to maintain confidence in the exam.
Failure to conduct the test in a "strict and fair manner" would bring disruption to South Korea "worse than a disaster", the country's Vice Education Minister, Choi Eun-ok, said.
"We believe we are in a situation where excessive measures are necessary,"
Wearable devices such as smart glasses, which can record test materials and provide information from AI, have also emerged as aids to cheaters across Asia.

The National Taiwan University disqualified a person in June from an entrance exam for allegedly using AI smart glasses to cheat, saying he was detected as he stared oddly at the test, according to local media.

An 18-year-old man in Japan also allegedly used smart glasses to photograph questions and seek answers via social media during a Waseda University entrance test in 2024, according to Japanese media reports.
"There have been growing concerns in Korea as well as in other East Asian countries about this issue," said Keita Takayama, professor and education scholar at Adelaide University.
"But the responses are quite remarkably different."
Stickers, rewards among anti-cheating measures
University entrance exams can be life-defining for students competing for places in the region's top institutions, Professor Takayama said.
He said there was a high premium on university reputation, which could determine career prospects.
"The name of the university follows you for the rest of your life,"
he said.

Philip Chan, a senior lecturer in education at Monash University, said an examination represented for many families not just a year of work but also a chance of getting into a good university and profession.
"When somebody cheats, a candidate who follows the rules has a reason to question whether they had a fair chance," Dr Chan said.
Before the Suneung last week, South Korean Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin said his ministry would inspect all students' glasses in exam sessions.

Authorities in South Korea said they would increase the number of supervisors, place stickers over buttons on clothing to stop exam-takers using hidden cameras, and told students not to bring their own pens and erasers.
The government offered a $US75,000 ($112,000) reward to people who outed cheaters.
Local media reported South Korean authorities also distributed aprons for students to wear in university admission exams at the weekend to block potential miniature cameras.
Students expressed anxiety about some of the anti-cheating measures before taking the Suneung.
"I'm worried I might panic if I have difficulty using the stationery provided during the test," Bang Min-ji, 18, told news agency AFP as she prepared to take the exam in central Seoul.
Song Ji-eun said she would struggle to concentrate "if supervisors keep checking my glasses" for tiny cameras.
"There's a saying that even a slight breeze can affect your focus, your score and even your entire life,"
she said.
Officials said they identified more than 100 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices, nearly half of which were detected through the three mobile phone alerts.
Earlier this week, Mr Choi resigned, saying he did not believe he was "immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance".
Korea's Ministry of Education declined to comment to the ABC.
How are other parts of Asia responding?
China's university entrance exam, called "gaokao", has similarly high stakes for the millions of people sitting it each year.
In June, the nation's Ministry of Education warned against bringing smart devices, including smart glasses, to the test, according to state media.

"Any candidate found carrying a device capable of transmitting or receiving information is considered to have cheated, resulting in the cancellation of their scores for all subjects and stages of the examinations they have registered," the Global Times reported.
In Japan, existing measures included having students turn their mobile phones off and put them in their bags before exams, Professor Takayama said.
However, cheating was perceived as remaining rare.
"In a room of 100 students, there would usually be four or five proctors walking around and closely watching them," he said.
"Although certainly generative AI and smart technology have made it a lot easier … it's still extremely difficult to [cheat]."
Rethinking exams after AI
Thomas Corbin, an associate professor of higher education at Deakin University, said he was concerned the risk posed by technology to exams would be ignored in Australia.
"We've not had the same reaction to wearable AI that we're seeing in Asia,"
Dr Corbin said.
He said the response of countries in Asia to tech-enabled cheating did not have to be a road map for Australia.
"The Australian context is different, and I think that we have an opportunity here to be making assessment better rather than just making assessment security better," he said.
"This moment is where we really need to rethink what we're trying to assess and how we're going to do it."

Australia's Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency had been working with higher education providers and supporting the sector to engage with generative AI, including in relation to academic integrity and assessment, a federal Department of Education spokesperson said.

"In relation to technology in schools, earlier this month all [state and federal] education ministers agreed that if schools are going to use technology, it should be used for a purpose rather than as a default," the spokesperson said.
"Ministers agreed to limits on screen use in schools, and restricting the student use of generative AI in primary schools and high school assessments."
Dr Chan, from Monash University, said there were ways of assessing students that would prevent them from relying on AI, such as having them deliver PowerPoint presentations.
"If the student knows the content, they will present very well,"
he said.
"If they don't know the content, they actually even don't know how to pronounce the vocabulary."
However, experts say the sit-down exam format remains deeply ingrained in East Asia, despite attempts to introduce different types of assessment.
"Because this competition is so intense, the system has to be absolutely fair," Professor Takayama said.
Sit-down exams were regarded as a fair method of assessing students because they involved standardised testing under similar conditions at the same time.
"The simultaneity is such a central part of fairness in the East Asian context," he said.
